method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry and caption. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch14 p778-782: auto-generated source checklist from existing 82 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 3x zoom; any printed unit errors or ambiguous glyphs are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan.

elements.source: Complete the classification flowchart of renal failure — 1) CKD  2) Non-CKD presenting over hours–days  3) Non-CKD presenting over days–weeks … A) Rapidly progressive renal failure (RPRF)  B) Chronic kidney disease  C) Acute kidney injury (AKI) [Flowchart: renal failure splits into CKD and non-CKD; non-CKD presenting over hours–days is AKI, and over days–weeks is rapidly progressive renal fail]
Rapidly progressive renal failure (RPRF) is defined in the flowchart by a presentation over: [The flowchart timings: AKI = hours to days; RPRF = days to weeks. (Book p778)]

Match each condition with its place in the renal-failure flowchart — 1) Acute tubular necrosis  2) Rapidly progressive GN  3) Hemolytic uremic syndrome  4) Atheroembolic renal disease … A) AKI (hours-days)  B) RPRF in some cases  C) RPRF due to glomerular pathology  D) RPRF [The flowchart puts acute tubular necrosis on the AKI (hours-days) limb, then lists for RPRF: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (due to glomerular]

Which of these is NOT listed as a cause of rapidly progressive renal failure? [ATN is the classic cause of AKI (hours–days), not of RPRF; RPRF causes listed are RPGN, HUS, severe AIN and atheroembolic renal disease. (Book p778)]

The flowchart attributes rapidly progressive renal failure chiefly to glomerular pathology. [Under RPRF the first listed cause is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), annotated 'due to glomerular pathology'. (Book p778)]
RPGN is defined as RPRF plus: [RPGN = RPRF + diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with crescents (an HPE/light-microscopy feature). (Book p778)]

Match each urine feature of RPGN with its description — 1) Colour  2) Output  3) Urine analysis … A) Cola-coloured (RBC present)  B) Decreased output  C) Proteinuria +/– (trace to variable) [RPGN urine: cola-coloured with RBCs; decreased output; urine examination shows proteinuria +/–. (Book p778)]

A 40-year-old man has a 3-week history of progressive puffiness around the eyes and legs, BP 160/100 mmHg, cola-coloured urine and reduced urine output. Which statement about these findings is correct? [RPGN features: periorbital puffiness, progressive oedema (extravascular compartment) and raised blood pressure, with cola-coloured urine and decreased]

Fill up: In RPGN, progressive oedema accumulates in the ______ compartment. [Features of RPGN: progressive oedema (extravascular compartment), periorbital puffiness and raised blood pressure. (Book p778)]
Raised blood pressure is a listed feature of RPGN along with periorbital puffiness. [RPGN features list ends with raised blood pressure. (Book p778)]
A man with RPGN is examined. Chest auscultation is expected to reveal: [Auscultation in RPGN: scattered crepitations (from fluid overload/uraemic lung). (Book p778)]

Which statement about blood investigations in RPGN is correct? [Blood investigations in RPGN: CBC normal; serum creatinine raised; serum urea raised; serum K⁺ normal or raised; ABG normal or metabolic acidosis. (Bo]

Match each RPGN investigation with its expected result — 1) CBC  2) Serum creatinine  3) Serum K⁺  4) ABG … A) Raised  B) Normal/raised  C) Normal  D) Normal/metabolic acidosis [RPGN investigations: CBC normal; creatinine raised; serum K⁺ normal or raised; ABG normal or metabolic acidosis (serum urea also raised). (Book p778)]

All but one of the following are typical laboratory findings in RPGN. Which is the odd one out? [The CBC is normal in RPGN; creatinine and urea are raised, serum K⁺ is normal or raised and the ABG is normal or shows metabolic acidosis. (Book p778)]

elements.source: The light-microscopy hallmark of crescentic glomerulonephritis described here is: [LM shows crescentic GN due to proliferation of parietal epithelial cells with fibrin; the number of crescents is an important factor. (Book p779)]

Fill up: The crescents of crescentic glomerulonephritis are formed by proliferation of ______ epithelial cells with fibrin. [Crescents arise from proliferation of parietal epithelial cells together with fibrin; their number matters prognostically. (Book p779)]

Match each immunofluorescence pattern in the biopsy figure with its image label — 1) No deposits  2) Uniform bright linear staining along the capillary walls  3) Coarse granular staining of capillary loops and mesangium … A) Diffuse granular IF  B) Linear IF  C) Negative IF [The figure panels are labelled: A. negative IF; B. diffuse granular IF; C. linear IF (with D. granular IF) — the linear pattern being the one written ]

Linear immunofluorescence in type I RPGN occurs because the antibodies are directed against a structural antigen of the glomerular basement membrane. [Type I RPGN (Goodpasture syndrome) shows linear IgG ± C3 along the glomerular capillary wall, being anti-GBM antibody disease; the granular patterns o]

Match each immunofluorescence finding with its important association as listed beside the biopsy panels — 1) Linear IF  2) Granular IF  3) Negative IF … A) No immune deposits (pauci-immune)  B) Diabetes mellitus and light chain disease  C) Goodpasture disease [The page lists Goodpasture disease (linear), diabetes mellitus and light chain disease (granular); panel A of the figure is a negative IF, which corre]

Which condition is NOT listed among the important associations of the immunofluorescence patterns? [The associations printed are Goodpasture disease (linear), diabetes mellitus and light chain disease (granular); PSGN is not on that list. (Book p779)]

A diabetic patient with nephrotic-range proteinuria and renal failure has a renal biopsy showing coarse granular immunofluorescence; the listed important association is: [Granular IF is importantly associated with diabetes mellitus and light chain disease; Goodpasture disease goes with linear IF. (Book p779)]

A patient with RPGN has a very high serum creatinine. The book advises against immediate renal biopsy because: [Note: biopsy should not be done if serum creatinine is markedly increased, as it may cause uremic bleeding. (Book p779)]

Arrange the correct sequence when the serum creatinine is very high — 1) First step  2) Then  3) If the value decreases … A) Dialysis  B) Biopsy  C) Recheck serum creatinine [When the creatinine is very high: first step dialysis → recheck serum creatinine → if the value decreases, proceed to biopsy. (Book p779)]
In the high-creatinine RPGN algorithm, biopsy is performed: [Algorithm: dialysis → recheck creatinine → biopsy if the value decreases (avoiding uremic bleeding from an immediate biopsy). (Book p779)]

According to the page, an immediately raised serum creatinine is an absolute contraindication to ever performing a renal biopsy. [It is the immediate biopsy that is avoided (uremic bleeding risk); after dialysis, if the creatinine decreases, biopsy is performed. (Book p779)]

elements.source: Match each first-line assessment in the RPGN treatment approach with what is sought — 1) ECG  2) ABG  3) Volume status … A) Signs of hyperkalemia  B) Inferior vena cava diameter on USG  C) Metabolic acidosis [Step 1 of the RPGN treatment approach: check ECG (signs of hyperkalaemia), ABG (metabolic acidosis) and volume status (IVC diameter on USG). (Book p78]

In the RPGN treatment algorithm, the ECG shows signs of hyperkalemia. The recommended treatment is: [ECG signs of hyperkalaemia in RPGN are treated with calcium gluconate IV 10 mL over 2–3 minutes. (Book p780)]
Calcium gluconate in hyperkalaemic RPGN is given as 10 mL IV over: [Calcium gluconate 10 mL IV given over 2–3 minutes for ECG signs of hyperkalaemia. (Book p780)]
A patient with RPGN has an ABG showing metabolic acidosis. Which treatments are listed in the algorithm? [ABG showing metabolic acidosis is treated with NaHCO₃ or dialysis. (Book p780)]

Fill up: In the RPGN treatment algorithm, volume status is assessed by the ______ diameter on ultrasound and treated with diuretics. [Volume status: check the inferior vena cava diameter on USG, the treatment being diuretics (with calcium gluconate for ECG signs of hyperkalaemia and ]

The first step in managing RPGN, before specific therapy, is to check the ECG, ABG and volume status. [Treatment approach, step 1: check ECG for hyperkalaemia, ABG for metabolic acidosis and volume status by IVC diameter on USG. (Book p780)]

All of the following are absolute (uremic) indications for dialysis EXCEPT: [Absolute uremic indications: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding and gastritis. Volume overload is a relative indication, alon]

Fill up: The absolute indications for dialysis in RPGN are all ______ in nature. [Absolute indications for dialysis = uremic: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding, gastritis. (Book p780)]

Match the dialysis indications in RPGN with their category — 1) Absolute indication  2) Relative indication  3) Qualifier for the relative group … A) Resistant to treatment  B) Uremic encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding, gastritis  C) Volume overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis [Absolute (uremic) indications: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding and gastritis. Relative indications: volume overload, hyper]

Hyperkalaemia in RPGN is an absolute indication for dialysis regardless of whether it responds to medical treatment. [Hyperkalaemia appears along with volume overload and metabolic acidosis under relative indications, qualified as resistant to treatment. (Book p780)]

On the basis of immunofluorescence, RPGN is classified into: [The TYPES flowchart of RPGN begins 'on the basis of immunofluorescence' and branches into type I (Goodpasture syndrome), type II (immune complex) and ]
Type I RPGN is also known as: [Type I / Goodpasture syndrome: IF shows linear IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall. (Book p780)]
Fill up: Type I RPGN shows ______ IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall on immunofluorescence. [Type I RPGN (Goodpasture syndrome) IF: linear IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall. (Book p780)]

Match each RPGN type with its label in the immunofluorescence flowchart — 1) Type II  2) Type III  3) Type II age note … A) Commonest below 20 years  B) Immune complex deposition  C) Pauci-immune, the commonest type [Type II = immune complex deposition (commonest in those below 20 years); type III = pauci-immune, marked m/c i.e. the commonest type overall. (Book p7]
Type II RPGN is commonest in patients: [Type II RPGN is annotated 'm/c in <20 yrs age' within the immune-complex branch. (Book p780)]

A 16-year-old girl has RPGN with immune-complex deposition on biopsy. Which example fits the book's type II list best? [Type II (immune complex) examples: SLE — underlined as the most important cause — Henoch–Schönlein purpura, IPGN (IgA predominant) and membranoprolife]

Systemic lupus erythematosus is marked as the most important cause within the type II RPGN examples. [In the type II branch, SLE is underlined with the note '(most important cause)'; HSP, IPGN (IgA predominant) and MPGN (10%) complete the list. (Book p]

Which example does NOT belong to the type II (immune complex) group of RPGN? [Microscopic polyangiitis belongs to type III (pauci-immune) with ANCA vasculitis and Wegener's granulomatosis. (Book p780)]

Match each type II (immune-complex) RPGN example with the note printed beside it — 1) Systemic lupus erythematosus  2) Henoch-Schönlein purpura and IPGN  3) Membranoproliferative GN … A) Adult variety  B) 10%  C) Most important cause [In the type II list SLE carries '(most important cause)', HSP with IPGN is bracketed as the adult variety, and MPGN is annotated 10%. (Book p780)]
Type III RPGN is described as: [Type III (pauci-immune) is marked m/c, i.e. the commonest type of RPGN, with examples ANCA vasculitis, Wegener's granulomatosis and microscopic polyan]

Which of these is NOT among the examples of type III (pauci-immune) RPGN? [IPGN (IgA predominant) is listed under type II immune-complex RPGN; type III pauci-immune examples are ANCA vasculitis, Wegener's granulomatosis and m]

Match the serology with its type in the double-positive versus double-negative table — 1) Anti-GBM + and ANCA +  2) Anti-GBM - and ANCA -  3) Prognosis of the double-positive type … A) Type V  B) Type IV  C) Good [Type IV is double positive (anti-GBM +, ANCA +) with a good prognosis; type V is double negative (anti-GBM -, ANCA -) with a poor prognosis. (Book p78]

Prognosis is good in double-positive (type IV) RPGN and poor in double-negative (type V) RPGN. [The table's prognosis row reads good for type IV (double positive) and poor for type V (double negative). (Book p780)]

A patient with RPGN has both anti-GBM antibody and ANCA positive on serology. According to the table he has: [Type IV = double positive (anti-GBM + and ANCA +), and this carries a good prognosis; type V (double negative) has a poor prognosis. (Book p780)]

elements.source: Pulmonary renal syndrome is defined as: [Pulmonary renal syndrome = RPGN (kidney involvement) + diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (lung involvement). (Book p781)]

All of the following are listed conditions under pulmonary renal syndrome EXCEPT: [Conditions listed: Goodpasture syndrome, microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and SLE (active disease). PSGN is not listed here.]
Active SLE is listed as one of the conditions causing pulmonary renal syndrome. [The conditions list for pulmonary renal syndrome ends with SLE (active disease). (Book p781)]

According to the note, RPGN with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and a non-specific antibody is: [Note: RPGN + DAH + antibody (non-specific) = anti-GBM disease; the antibody in question is anti-GBM. (Book p781)]

Fill up: Goodpasture disease is RPGN + diffuse alveolar haemorrhage + antibody against the noncollagenous domain of the ______ chain of type-IV collagen. [Goodpasture disease = RPGN + DAH + antibody against the noncollagenous domain of the α3 chain of type-IV collagen. (Book p781)]

Fill up: Besides smoking, hydrocarbon exposure and lung infection, the fourth 2nd/trigger factor listed for Goodpasture disease is ______. [2nd/trigger factors for Goodpasture disease: smoking, hydrocarbon exposure, fluid overload and lung infection. (Book p781)]

Which is NOT a listed trigger for Goodpasture disease? [Listed triggers: smoking, hydrocarbon exposure, fluid overload and lung infection. A streptococcal sore throat relates to PSGN, not Goodpasture diseas]
Which HLA pair carries the highest risk in Goodpasture disease? [HLA association in Goodpasture disease: high risk DR2/15 and DR4; low risk DR1 and DR7. (Book p781)]

A 25-year-old heavy smoker has haemoptysis, a fall in Hb and rapidly rising creatinine; anti-GBM antibody is positive. Which HLA type would be expected to increase his risk? [High-risk HLA types in Goodpasture disease are DR2/15 and DR4; DR1 and DR7 are low risk. (Book p781)]
Which HLA type is protective/low-risk in Goodpasture disease rather than high-risk? [Low-risk HLA types: DR1 and DR7. High risk: DR2/15 and DR4. (Book p781)]
The first session of dialysis should be kept shorter than: [Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: the first session of dialysis should be <1 hour, with subsequent sessions of 4 hours. (Book p781)]
The duration of subsequent dialysis sessions recommended after the first short session is: [First session <1 hour; subsequent sessions 4 hours, to avoid dialysis disequilibrium syndrome. (Book p781)]

Complete the dialysis disequilibrium flowchart — 1) Urea in the blood compartment  2) Effect on blood osmolality  3) Consequence in cells … A) Cerebral edema → seizure, death  B) ↓ Osmolality  C) Rapidly moves to the dialysate compartment [Flowchart: urea rapidly moves from blood to dialysate → blood osmolality falls → water moves into cells → cerebral oedema → seizure and death. (Book p]

Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome occurs because urea is removed so quickly that the osmolality of the blood compartment falls. [Urea moves rapidly into the dialysate, dropping blood osmolality; water then moves into cells, producing cerebral oedema with seizure and death if dia]

A severely uraemic patient receives a 4-hour first dialysis session and develops headache, confusion and a seizure. The mechanism is: [Dialysis disequilibrium: rapid urea removal → ↓ blood osmolality → water moves into cells (including brain) → cerebral oedema, seizure and death. (Boo]

Which statement correctly summarises the prevention of dialysis disequilibrium syndrome? [Prevention: the first dialysis session should be <1 hour; subsequent sessions are 4 hours, because continuing beyond 2 hours risks cerebral oedema. (B]

elements.source: Lung involvement (as opposed to renal involvement) occurs in what proportion of Goodpasture patients? [Presentation flowchart: lung involvement 75% versus renal involvement 'as %', with renal involvement indicating a poor prognosis. (Book p782)]
In Goodpasture syndrome, renal involvement is associated with a poor prognosis. [The flowchart places 'renal involvement (as %)' with the note poor prognosis. (Book p782)]

A young man presents with 2 weeks of cough and haemoptysis. He has no fever and no comorbidity. Which listed feature supports the diagnosis of Goodpasture lung involvement? [Lung features: history of smoking, cough, haemoptysis, and no fever or comorbidity — the absence of fever is emphasised. (Book p782)]

All but one of the following are listed lung features of Goodpasture syndrome. Which is the odd one out? [The book specifically notes 'no fever, comorbidity' among the lung features of Goodpasture syndrome. (Book p782)]

Match the investigation with its stated result — 1) DLCO  2) X-ray chest  3) CT scan … A) ↑ (increased)  B) Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage  C) B/L diffuse infiltrate [Evaluation: DLCO is ↑ (increased); X-ray shows bilateral diffuse infiltrate; CT scan shows diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. (Book p782)]

The chest X-ray in Goodpasture syndrome shows a bilateral diffuse infiltrate, marked by an arrow in the figure. [The chest X-ray figure is labelled 'B/L diffuse infiltrate' with an arrow pointing to it. (Book p782)]

A patient with haemoptysis and RPGN has a CT chest showing bilateral ground-glass with dependent consolidation. The figure labels this: [The two CT panels on the page are labelled 'diffuse alveolar haemorrhage'. (Book p782)]

Which evaluation finding is NOT part of the Goodpasture work-up as printed? [The DLCO in Goodpasture syndrome is increased (↑), reflecting the presence of blood in the alveoli; X-ray shows B/L diffuse infiltrate and CT shows di]

The serum creatinine cut-off below which active management is indicated, provided urine output is normal, is: [Condition 2 requiring active management: Sr. creatinine <5.5 mg/dL with normal urine output. (Book p782)]

A new cellular crescent, as opposed to a fibrous crescent, is one of the conditions requiring active management. [Condition 3: a new cellular crescent (non-fibrous) requires active management, since fibrous crescents represent old, irreversible scarring. (Book p78]
The treatment listed for Goodpasture disease/pulmonary renal syndrome is: [Treatment: mainstay PLEX (plasma exchange) + steroid and cyclophosphamide for 3–6 months. (Book p782)]
The listed duration of steroid and cyclophosphamide treatment with plasma exchange is: [Mainstay PLEX + steroid and cyclophosphamide for 3–6 months. (Book p782)]

A patient with Goodpasture syndrome has completed treatment and is anti-GBM antibody negative. He asks about definitive treatment. The book's answer is: [Definitive treatment: renal transplant, performed after the antibody has been negative for 6 months. (Book p782)]

In Goodpasture syndrome there is no recurrence of the disease after renal transplantation. [Note: in Goodpasture syndrome there is no recurrence after renal transplant — in contrast to Alport syndrome, where the α3 defect gives a 5% chance of]

[Note: in Alport syndrome, due to the α3 (collagen) defect there is a 5% chance of Goodpasture syndrome after renal transplant — unlike Goodpasture syn]

Fill up: In Alport syndrome, the post-transplant risk of Goodpasture syndrome is ______%. [Alport syndrome carries a 5% chance of Goodpasture syndrome after renal transplant because of the α3 chain defect. (Book p782)]
